notes.title: Check the sign on the screen
notes.text: The captions near the final line do not reliably preserve the slope’s sign. The attendance model decreases, so a corresponding logarithmic regression should have a negative slope; verify the actual calculator display before copying a numerical equation.

ican.text: I can linearise exponential and power models using logarithm laws.
I can identify which transformed variables to plot and interpret the resulting slope and intercept.
I can recover a model in the original variables from a fitted transformed line.
I can check domain restrictions and use the correct logarithm base when reversing a transformation.
I can interpret predictions and limitations in the original context.

ku.text: For $y=ab^x$ with $a,b>0$, taking natural logs gives $\ln y=\ln a+x\ln b$. A plot of $\ln y$ against $x$ has slope $\ln b$ and intercept $\ln a$.
If $\ln y=mx+c$, reverse the transformation to obtain $y=e^c(e^m)^x$. Thus $a=e^c$ and $b=e^m$.
For $y=ax^b$ with $a>0$ and $x>0$, $\ln y=\ln a+b\ln x$. A plot of $\ln y$ against $\ln x$ has slope $b$ and intercept $\ln a$.
The same structure works with base-10 logarithms: if $\log_{10}y=m\log_{10}x+c$, then $y=10^c x^m$. Match the inverse operation to the logarithm base.
Logarithms require positive arguments. For log–log plots both observed $x$ and $y$ must be positive; for a plot of $\log y$ against $x$, the observed $y$ values must be positive.
The slope of a log–log plot is the power exponent. For an exponential model the slope of $\ln y$ against $x$ is $\ln b$, not $b$.
A straight pattern in transformed data can support a proposed model but does not prove it. Interpret residuals on the relevant scale and be cautious when predicting beyond the observed range.
Changing the logarithm base changes intercepts and exponential-model slopes, but the exponent obtained from a log–log plot is unchanged when the same base is used on both axes.

misc.weak: The intercept on a $\ln y$ graph is $a$.
misc.better: The intercept is $\ln a$. Recover $a$ by applying the exponential function.

misc.weak: The slope on a $\ln y$ against $x$ graph is the growth factor.
misc.better: The slope is $\ln b$, so the factor is $b=e^{\text{slope}}$.

misc.weak: Use $e^c$ to undo an intercept from a base-10 log graph.
Take $\ln(0)$ before fitting the transformed line.
misc.better: Zero and negative values have no real logarithm. Check whether the transformation is valid for every observation.

misc.weak: A straight log–log graph proves a power law holds for all inputs.
misc.better: It supports a power model over the observed range; assess residuals, context and extrapolation separately.

terms.text: Transforming variables so a proposed nonlinear relationship becomes linear in the transformed variables.
A plot in which one variable is represented on a logarithmic scale or transformed using a logarithm.
A plot involving logarithms of both variables; a power relationship becomes linear.
Returning from transformed variables to the original variables using the corresponding inverse operation.

worked.prompt: A researcher models a positive quantity $y$ against time $x$. A linear regression of $Y=\ln y$ against $x$ gives $Y=1.2-0.3x$ over the observed interval $0\leq x\leq5$.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find the exponential model in the original variables.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Interpret the initial value and the change per unit of time.
parts.a: At $x=0$, the predicted initial quantity is $e^{1.2}\approx3.32$ units. Each time unit multiplies the prediction by $e^{-0.3}\approx0.741$, corresponding to a decrease of about $25.9\%$ per time unit.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Predict $y$ when $x=4$ and identify whether this is interpolation.
parts.a: $y=e^{1.2-0.3(4)}=e^0=1$. Since $4$ lies within the observed interval, this is interpolation.

parts.label: d
parts.q: A different experiment yields $\log_{10}y=1.5\log_{10}x+0.6$ for positive $x$. Find its original power model.
parts.a: Taking powers of $10$ gives $y=10^{0.6}x^{1.5}\approx3.98x^{1.5}$. The exponent is the transformed slope, while the coefficient is $10$ raised to the intercept.

parts.label: e
parts.q: Explain why the model from part (a) needs caution at $x=20$.
parts.a: Twenty lies outside the observed interval, so this is extrapolation. The fitted rate may not remain constant that far beyond the data.

kq.q: Which graph helps test an exponential model?
kq.model: For positive outputs, plot $\ln y$ against $x$. A straight pattern is consistent with $y=ab^x$, with slope $\ln b$ and intercept $\ln a$.

kq.q: Which graph helps test a power model?
kq.model: For positive inputs and outputs, plot $\ln y$ against $\ln x$. Its slope estimates the exponent and its intercept estimates $\ln a$.

kq.q: Why must the logarithm base be retained in the working?
kq.model: The inverse of $\ln$ is the exponential function $e^x$, while the inverse of $\log_{10}$ is $10^x$.
